extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examiners on evaluating whether claimed inventions meet statutory patentability requirements (especially 35 U.S.C. 101, 112, 102, 103) and on properly documenting and communicating findings in Office actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must disclose the best mode in such a manner that a person of ordinary skill in the art could practice the best mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2165 et seq. for additional guidance. Deficiencies related to disclosure of the best mode are not usually encountered during examination because evidence to support such a deficiency is seldom in the record (citing Fonar Corp. v. General Elec. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 analysis (novelty and obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review begins with a comparison of the claimed subject matter to what is known in the prior art; if no differences are found the claim lacks novelty under 35 U.S.C. 102; if differences exist they must be assessed in light of a person of ordinary skill to determine obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§ 2131-2146 and §§ 2150-2159 for specific guidance on patentability determinations. Differences identified must be assessed against knowledge possessed by a person of ordinary skill in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly communicate findings and bases in Office actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should confirm a prima facie case of unpatentability exists before imposing a rejection and the Office action should clearly communicate the findings, conclusions and reasons which support them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the applicable form paragraphs in Office actions to state the basis for any objections or rejections to reduce the chance of a misunderstanding as to the grounds of objection or rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 101 statutory scope (four categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention must come within one of the four statutory categories set forth by 35 U.S.C. 101: process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter (or a useful improvement thereof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2106.03 for a discussion of the four categories. Establishing that the claim falls within a statutory category is the first criterion of subject matter eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double patenting prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor may obtain only one patent for the same invention; identical subject matter claimed in more than one application to the same inventive entity is barred and forms the basis for statutory double patenting rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 804 for a full discussion. Use form paragraphs 8.30, 8.31 and 8.32 for statutory double patenting rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming and correctness of inventor(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventor(s) must be properly identified in the application (rules differ for applications filed before and after September 16, 2012); incorrect inventorship should be addressed and corrected when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2109 for inventorship discussion and MPEP § 602.01(c) et seq. for correction of inventorship. In rare clear situations where correct inventorship is not named and no request to correct has been filed, the examiner should reject claims under appropriate statutory provisions (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 101 and 115 for AIA, or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter eligibility two-criteria framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Two criteria govern subject matter eligibility: (a) the claim must fall within one of the four statutory categories; and (b) the claim must not be directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon/product of nature) unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2106.03 and § 2106.04 for detailed information. Judicial exceptions are limited to abstract ideas, laws of nature, and natural phenomena (including products of nature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility requirement (35 U.S.C. 101 utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention must be useful and have a utility that is specific, substantial and credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejection for lack of utility is appropriate when (1) it is not apparent why the invention is useful because the applicant failed to identify any specific and substantial utility and there is no well established utility, or (2) an asserted specific and substantial utility is not credible. Rejections for lack of utility should not be based on frivolousness, fraudulence, or public policy. See MPEP § 2107 and subsections for form paragraphs and precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atomic Energy Act bar
rubrics_metrics.description: No patent shall be granted for any invention which is useful solely in the utilization of special nuclear material or atomic energy in an atomic weapon (42 U.S.C. 2181(a) etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications disclosing or appearing to disclose inventions relating to atomic energy are reported to the Department of Energy under 37 CFR 1.14(d); all rejections under sections of the Atomic Energy Act must be made only by Licensing and Review personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Living subject matter eligibility principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Living subject matter may be patent-eligible if directed to a statutory category and not excluded as a product of nature; nature-based products may be eligible if they possess 'markedly different characteristics from any found in nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Chakrabarty (genetically engineered bacterium) and related case law (e.g., Myriad, Roslin) for analysis. See MPEP § 2106.04(b) subsection II for products of nature discussion and § 2106.04(c) for 'markedly different characteristics' analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human organisms excluded from patentability (AIA sec. 33(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to or encompassing a human organism are excluded from patentability; the broadest reasonable interpretation of a claim that encompasses a human organism must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 and AIA sec. 33(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 7.04.03 to reject a claim under 35 U.S.C. 101 and section 33(a). Precede this paragraph with form paragraph 7.04.01 which quotes 35 U.S.C. 101, and in the Office action explain why the claim is interpreted to read on a human organism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Alice/Mayo two-part framework for judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Alice/Mayo two-part test is the required framework: (Step 2A) determine whether claims are directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon; (Step 2B) if so, determine whether the claim recites additional elements amounting to significantly more than the judicial exception (the 'inventive concept').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Alice/Mayo test is the only test that should be used to evaluate eligibility of claims under examination. Other tests (e.g., machine-or-transformation, 'useful, concrete, and tangible' result, In re Alappat 'special purpose computer' test) are not standalone tests and should be considered only as part of the integration or 'significantly more' analysis. See MPEP § 2106.04 and § 2106.05 for detailed guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction: establish broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim as a whole prior to examining for eligibility; claim interpretation sets coverage boundaries and influences whether claims fall within statutory categories or encompass exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining BRI is essential and claim interpretation affects both criteria for eligibility and the Alice/Mayo analysis. See MPEP § 2111 for more information. Examples (Mentor Graphics, Synopsys, Enfish, Amdocs) illustrate how construction can change eligibility outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the eligibility flowchart and Pathways A/B/C
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the provided flowchart to determine eligibility: Step 1 (statutory category), Step 2A (directed to judicial exception?), Step 2B (significantly more?). Claims eligible via Pathway A (streamlined/self-evident), Pathway B (not directed to a judicial exception), or Pathway C (directed to exception but recite significantly more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If uncertain whether streamlined analysis (Pathway A) applies, conduct the full eligibility analysis. If a claim is not eligible via any pathway, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101. The flowchart promotes examination efficiency and consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete examination across statutory requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of whether a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 is made, a complete examination should be made for every claim under each patentability requirement: 35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, and issues like utility, inventorship, and double patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2103. The §101 inquiry is a threshold test and other requirements must also be evaluated to ensure the claim meets all conditions and requirements of the Patent Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of form paragraphs and examiner notes in Office actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should utilize prescribed form paragraphs (e.g., for double patenting, human organism rejections, lack of utility) and include examiner notes/bracket instructions to properly format and explain rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: use form paragraphs 8.30-8.32 for statutory double patenting; form paragraph 7.04.03 (preceded by 7.04.01) for human organism rejections; see MPEP subsections for bracket instructions and explanatory text.
